newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Westpac Australia leading index falls in Dec.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Westpac Australia leading index falls in Dec.

text.p: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute leading index of Australian economic activity, which indicates where activity will be in six to nine months time, fell by 0.3 points or 0.2 percent in December, Westpac said on Wednesday.
The coincident index, which measures current economic activity, fell by 1.5 points or 0.9 percent in December.
The leading index of inflation fell by 0.4 of one point to 4.3 percent in December.
"After recent solid rises, the small fall does not change the positive message from the leading index," said Bill Evans, Westpac's General Manager Economic Strategy & Planning.
The fall in the index follows a sharp 0.7 percent increase in November which was mainly due to a sharp gain in non-residential construction approvals relating to Olympic projects, he said.
"With no similar large approvals in December non-residential approvals fell 28 percent," he added.
Evans said the best way to assess the leading index was the smoothed growth rate which still rose at a 2.6 percent pace and averaged 3.0 percent in the December quarter.
Westpac said this was well up on the 1.1 percent of the first nine months of 1996 and a growth rate not seen since the September quarter 1994.
The fall in the coincident index which was being driven by retail sales and employment, confirmed current activity was very weak in the December quarter.
The leading index flags only a moderate recovery in the first half of 1997.
"However, by the second half the leading index suggests economic conditions should be looking much healthier," he said.
The leading index of inflation fell to its lowest level since late 1994 and continued to suggest only very moderate inflationary pressures.
Underlying inflation, which fell to 2.1 percent in the December quarter, looked set to stay at the low end of the Reserve Bank's target range of 2.0-3.0 percent through 1997, Westpac said.
Evans expected that with inflationary pressures subdued, the full CPI would benefit significantly from the 0.7 percent cut in banks' mortgage rates announced in the past week.
"This could reduce the annual growth rate in the CPI from 1.5 percent to below 0.5 percent in the June quarter and will help entrench low inflation expectations," Evans added.
